standard_prerequisites.name: Minimal numerical types of genus at least two and the classification of their proper subgraphs
standard_prerequisites.statement: A numerical type is a tuple of an integer n and integer families of multiplicities, intersection numbers, weights and genera subject to the five defining conditions of the chapter, and it is minimal when no index has genus zero and self-intersection equal to the negative of its weight; the genus of the type is the alternating sum determined by those data. The chapter classifies the proper subgraphs of the intersection graph of a minimal type of genus at least two, up to the possible shapes, and proves the auxiliary estimates on the entries of that graph that the proof uses. The author's own lemmas and proposition of the same chapter are the allowed inputs.
standard_prerequisites.use: The counted lemma is the quantitative estimate that makes the classification of minimal types of fixed genus finite, and the chapter's enumeration of minimal types of low genus depends on it.

core_obligations: Reduce to a single entry: by the chapter's elementary bound it is enough to show the assertion for one distinguished intersection number, so the estimate for all weighted entries follows from the bound for that one (source line 4178).

Normalise the data: the author records that no vertex has positive self-intersection in a minimal type of genus at least two, and that the multiplicities and the entries satisfy the recurrence conditions, which allows the intersection graph to be treated as a graph with nonnegative weights on its edges (source lines 4180-4220).

Use the classification: the proper subgraphs of that graph are then matched one by one against the shapes classified by the author's proposition, and for each shape the author derives the corresponding numerical inequality between the entry in question and the genus (source lines 4220-4260).

Sum up the contributions: the inequalities coming from the individual shapes are combined with the auxiliary bounds on the remaining entries to produce the stated constant, which is the largest of the constants appearing in the case analysis (source lines 4260-4283).

proof_roadmap.step: Reduce the assertion to a bound for one distinguished entry.
Normalise the graph data using the recurrence conditions and the sign of the self-intersections.
Match the proper subgraphs to the classified shapes and derive the inequalities case by case.
Combine the case inequalities into the stated constant.
